Sawyer Merritt (@SawyerMerritt)

Canaccord Genuity analyst George Gianarikas says those who viewed @Tesla’s Q3 earnings call negatively are “flatly wrong.”

"The tea-leaf readers whispering about a 'subdued' tone on the call are flatly wrong, in our opinion. This was one of the most unapologetically bullish Tesla calls in many a moon.

Think about it, on the call management said that:
• EVs have their highest backlog in 4 years, with Musk adding that "...we are producing and delivering as many cars as we can...".
• FSD attach rates surged to over 75% of new vehicle deliveries in North America (nearly a 20% QoQ increase), with active subscriptions reaching 1.74 million. Whoa.
• High-volume manufacturing of Optimus is officially underway in Fremont, yielding the company’s first production-grade humanoid robots built on a standard assembly line.
• Energy storage demand is "very strong" with Musk adding "We're actually almost sold out of all Megapacks for 2027, and we're ramping production as quickly as possible to meet demand. We also expect gross margins on that to increase meaningfully."
• Not to mention recent launches of the Cybercab, Tesla Semi, and Roadster (with the latter unlikely to be needle-moving).

Call us biased, but between that conference call commentary and shiny new product drops, Tesla appears to be dripping with growth potential. Count us in."

George reiterated a $442 price target for $TSLA.

At an all-hands, Zuck said he initially didn’t want to watch it—but if he was going to, we’d all watch it together

So the whole company saw the movie together in a rented out theatre

Afterwards we threw an impromptu company party across several bars in Palo Alto

Sean then says: “Appletinis all around!”

After the movie, I was standing next to Zuck at the party and asked him: “wouldn’t it be funny if we ordered appletinis?”

Zuck loved the idea. A hilarious way to toast to an incredibly inaccurate movie

And so this is one of my favorite photos from my time at Facebook

Our definition of crashes is so loose with autonomous vehicles. Going through a pothole is not a car crash 😂


TeslaZoa (@TeslaZoa)

Tesla has reported the first Cybercab crash to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).

According to the report, a Cybercab was traveling at approximately 5 mph (8 km/h) when it drove into a large, water-filled pothole, causing damage to the vehicle.

Personally, I don't think this incident should be viewed in the same way as a typical traffic accident.

At the time, a safety monitor was inside the vehicle, and there were no passengers.

While the vehicle sustained damage and the incident was officially reported as a crash, I believe it makes more sense to view this as an edge case encountered during autonomous driving development and testing.

After all, identifying and learning from these unusual scenarios is an essential part of improving autonomous driving technology and making it safer and more reliable.

Great to see NHTSA working so hard to modernize the rules for vehicles like Cybercab. I guess now we know why they brought the turn signal sounds back


Sawyer Merritt (@SawyerMerritt)

NHTSA announced today that they are proposing new rules aimed at removing U.S. federal regulatory barriers for autonomous vehicles without steering wheels or pedals, such as @Tesla's Cybercab.

The proposed changes include:
• Eliminating requirements for manually operated turn signal controls in vehicles without steering wheels or pedals: "NHTSA has concluded that the self-canceling and manually operated control requirements in the current standard are unnecessary for turn signal operating units that are installed on vehicles without manually operated driving controls."

• Allowing autonomous driving systems to control turn signals, hazard lights, and high/low beams without traditional driver-operated switches.

• Removing certain dashboard indicator requirements for turn signals and high beams in vehicles without manual driving controls.

• Allowing optional cyan-colored exterior lights to indicate when a vehicle is operating autonomously, with standardized requirements for their placement, brightness, and operation.

• Eliminating outdated restrictions on vertical headlight arrangements, giving automakers greater design flexibility.

• Allowing modern integrated headlights to be tested at manufacturer-specified voltages rather than requiring 12.8 volts.

NHTSA says the changes are intended to eliminate unnecessary regulatory barriers, reduce costs, and enable innovation without compromising vehicle safety.











— https://nitter.kareem.one/SawyerMerritt/status/2113653202004455443#m
tweets.text_zh:
很高兴看到 NHTSA 如此努力地使 Cyber​​cab 等车辆的规则现代化。我想现在我们知道为什么他们把转向灯声音带回来了


索耶·梅里特（@SawyerMerritt）

NHTSA 今天宣布，他们正在提出新规则，旨在消除美国联邦对没有方向盘或踏板的自动驾驶汽车（例如 @Tesla 的 Cybercab）的监管障碍。

拟议的变更包括：
• 消除不带方向盘或踏板的车辆中对手动操作转向信号控制装置的要求：“NHTSA 得出的结论是，对于安装在不带手动操作驾驶控制装置的车辆上的转向信号操作装置，当前标准中的自取消和手动操作控制要求是不必要的。”

• 允许自动驾驶系统控制转向灯、危险警示灯和远光/近光，而无需传统的驾驶员操作开关。

• 取消了没有手动驾驶控制装置的车辆中转向灯和远光灯的某些仪表板指示器要求。

• 允许使用可选的青色车外灯来指示车辆何时自主运行，并对其位置、亮度和操作提出标准化要求。

• 消除对垂直前灯布置的过时限制，为汽车制造商提供更大的设计灵活性。

• 允许在制造商指定的电压下测试现代集成车头灯，而不是要求 12.8 伏。

NHTSA 表示，这些变化旨在消除不必要的监管障碍、降低成本并在不影响车辆安全的情况下实现创新。

People First's anti-robotaxi website shares a strong production trail with an Uber-funded campaign (CAR)

Public website records connect People First Transportation Alliance's site with Citizens for Affordable Rates, which disclosed $11.6 million from Uber in the first half of 2026. They don't identify who commissioned or paid for People First's site.

People First Transportation Alliance has spent the fall campaigning against robotaxis in Washington, D.C. The RSVP page for its Oct 6 rally at the Wilson Building reads "People First, Not Robotaxis," and its flyer reads "Against Waymo's Robotaxis." On Oct 19, the Washington Post asked who is behind the group, and several listed "founding members" told the Post they aren't part of it.

I went through the group's website: code, image files, timestamps and domain records, plus the lobbying filings of the people around it. I couldn't find a document that says who pays People First's bills, and I've filed three public records requests that might turn one up. What the records do show is a production trail linking People First's website to the website of Citizens for Affordable Rates, a New York advocacy group whose filings name Uber as its only disclosed funder.

- Shared accounts. Both sites' posts are credited to the same Squarespace author account. People First's site was created by an account created at the same second that author ID encodes.
- Shared designer. Both sites' logos carry the same named Canva design identity, "pamela.stamoulis." So does a billboard ad for Citizens for Affordable Rates (CAR).
- A shared date. One People First post carries the exact anomalous date of a CAR post, down to the millisecond. That strongly suggests a reused post or a common source.

Citizens for Affordable Rates (CAR) launched in January 2025 as an "Uber-led coalition" to cut New York's car insurance costs. Its filing for January–June 2026 lists $11,615,454 from Uber, the only funder disclosed in that filing.

Amelia Adams, a New York consultant and former registered Uber lobbyist, told the Post she helps run People First. CAR's January–June 2026 filing lists expense rows to her firm, Adams Advisors, totaling $213,872 for "civic engagement/community organizing." Two of those rows share the same date and amount, so the actual total paid may be lower. Adams and Uber told the Post that this work is unrelated to autonomous vehicles or People First. Uber also said it wasn't involved in People First's website or its D.C. protest.

1. The same accounts appear on both sites

Squarespace sites expose internal data to anyone who adds `?format=json` to a page address. Comparing that data:

- The same author account. All four of People First's news posts, and 134 of CAR's 192 posts, are credited to one Squarespace author account (ID `558b041e…`).
- The same creator account. People First's site settings include a field recording when the account that created the site was itself created: June 24, 2015, 19:25:18 UTC. That matches, to the second, the time encoded in the author ID. A profile created just for one site would carry a much later date. So the account that created People First's site is very likely the same account credited with CAR's posts.
- The same designer. People First's logo and favicon, and seven CAR image files from five Canva designs, carry embedded Canva export data with the same user ID and the name "pamela.stamoulis." One of them is a CAR billboard ad (more below).

The Post first reported the "pamela.stamoulis" username, noted that a digital strategist named Pamela Stamoulis has ties to New York and Washington, and said she didn't respond. Federal campaign-finance records show a Pamela Stamoulis paid as staff by Senate Majority PAC in 2017–18 and by Biden for President in 2019–20. She lists herself as a self-employed consultant on donation records since 2021.

2. A People First post carries a CAR post's anomalous date

Every Squarespace post has a visible date field the author can change. On CAR's site, clipped news stories are often backdated to the original article's date.

- May 12, 2025. CAR's site gets a clip of New York Post letters about Councilman Yusef Salaam. Its date field is set to Jan 17, 2024, 3:21 p.m. That date is wrong for the clip, since the letters ran almost two weeks later. The system stores it as `1705522860395`.
- People First's site. Its New York Post story about California drivers protesting Waymo, from January 2026, carries the same date value, `1705522860395`, down to the millisecond. No other CAR post has it.

A match that precise isn't a coincidence. Together with the shared accounts, it strongly suggests the People First post started as a reused CAR post, or that both came from a common source. The public records don't show how it was copied. A direct duplicate, an intermediate copy, a template or an import could each preserve the value. None of the Salaam text remains.

What about January? Three of People First's other posts have date fields reading Jan 10, 2026, 1:27–1:34 p.m. That's shortly after the articles they clip were published; the newest went up at 11:15 a.m. that day. The copied post's thumbnail is a file named "Screenshot 2026-01-10 at 11.53.03." That's consistent with the clips being made on Jan 10, months before People First had a website. But date fields can survive copying and file names can be kept, so it doesn't prove when the Waymo text was written. The posts' internal IDs point to May 3, 2026, the day after People First's site was created; all four were created within 14 seconds of each other.

3. The same design account made CAR's billboard

One of CAR's images carries the same Canva identity and is titled "FINAL_CAR_SOMOS_BILLBOARDS_1728 x 512 px." It reads "Car insurance is fueling our affordability crisis" and "Paid For By Citizens For Affordable Rates." CAR announced a "six-figure ad campaign" aimed at New York officials attending the SOMOS conference in Puerto Rico in November 2025.

That ties the billboard's design file to the same named Canva identity as People First's logo. It doesn't show who bought the ads or ran the campaign.

CAR's lobbying report for July–December 2025 lists $8,489 in expenses, none of them a separately identified SOMOS ad buy. It also says CAR didn't have to name its funders that period because it was under the spending threshold.

4. Author names changed on both sites

When the Post reported its story, the site's metadata credited the posts to an author named "Pamela" with the display name "PS," and the Post says it asked Pamela Stamoulis for comment several times. By 11:31 a.m. ET on Oct 19, the morning the story ran, fresh copies of both sites showed "Misc" instead. Archived copies show "PS" as late as mid-September, so the change came sometime between then and that morning. Public data doesn't show the exact day, or why it was made.

There was one timestamped change on the evening of Oct 19. At 9:36 p.m. ET, a CAR post's author was switched from a second account, displayed as "Laila ElGohary," to the shared "Misc" account. The post's text didn't change. By late that night, that second account's display name read "TJ." I can't say who made these changes or why.

5. Overlapping organizations

CAR's press releases and People First's own materials name some of the same organizations and people:

- Rev. Conrad Tillard signed a CAR clergy letter and is quoted in its releases. He's a listed People First member and, per the Post, recruited clergy for its Albany trip.
- New York Communities for Change appears in both.
- The Yemeni American Merchants Association is quoted in CAR's January 2026 coalition release. It's named under "Standing together" on People First's D.C. rally RSVP page.

You can verify this yourself:
- Open `peoplefirsttranspo.com/news?…` and find the New York Post post. Its `"publishOn"` value is `1705522860395`.
- Open `citizensforaffordablerates.c…` and page to the oldest post, the Salaam letters clip. It has the same value.
- Open `peoplefirsttranspo.com/?form…` and find `creatorAccountCreationDate`: `1435173918522` (June 24, 2015, 19:25:18 UTC). The first eight characters of the author ID, `558b041e`, convert from hexadecimal to the same second.
